title: Cadmus et Harmonia
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Cadmus, who does not know that his daughter and his small grandson have become gods of the sea, is driven out of the city he founded by grief, by a run of disasters and by the portents he has seen, and wanders as far as the borders of Illyria with his wife. Old there, going back over the beginnings of his house in talk, he asks aloud whether the serpent he once ran through was sacred, and prays to be made a serpent himself — and the prayer is granted in the words he used to make it. Ovid then follows the change part by part, in order: scales over the hardening skin, the legs fusing and tapering, the arms held out for one last touch, and only then the tongue splitting and the voice going to a hiss. His wife beats her breast, asks the gods above to change her too, and strokes the crested neck; the part closes with two snakes gliding into a nearby wood, gentle to human beings ever since.

sentences.t:
Nescit Agenorides natam parvumque nepotem
aequoris esse deos:
sentences.l: Agenor's son does not know that [his] daughter and [his] small grandson are gods of the sea:
sentences.i: Agenor's son does not know that his daughter and his little grandson have become gods of the sea:
sentences.n: Agenorides, “the son of Agenor”, stands in for the name Cadmus, which arrives only at 572. A patronymic in -ides is a normal way for Latin verse to name a man, and Ovid uses it as freely as the name itself — you will meet dozens across the poem. The construction is indirect statement: nescit governs an accusative subject (natam, nepotem) with the infinitive esse, where English needs “that” and a finite verb. The daughter and grandson are not named here; they belong to the tale just finished.

sentences.t:
luctu serieque malorum
victus et ostentis, quae plurima viderat, exit
conditor urbe sua, tamquam fortuna locorum,
non sua se premeret;
sentences.l: overcome by grief and by the string of evils and by the portents, of which he had seen very many, the founder goes out from his own city, as though the fortune of the places, and not his own, were pressing on him;
sentences.i: broken by grief, by one disaster after another, and by the portents he had seen in such numbers, the founder walks out of his own city — as though it were the luck of the place that bore down on him, and not his own;
sentences.n: conditor, “founder”, sits where the name would go: the man who built the city is identified by that act at the moment he abandons it. quae plurima viderat is Latin's habit of hanging the adjective on the relative pronoun — literally “which, very many, he had seen”, where English wants “of which he had seen a great many”. tamquam takes the subjunctive premeret because the comparison is unreal: he only supposes it is the place's bad luck.

sentences.t:
longisque erroribus actus
contigit Illyricos profuga cum coniuge fines.
sentences.l: and driven by long wanderings he touched the Illyrian borders with [his] fugitive wife.
sentences.i: and driven by long wandering he reached the borders of Illyria, his wife an exile beside him.
sentences.n: profuga is feminine and agrees with coniuge, not with the subject: Ovid gives the word “fugitive” to the wife, so that her exile is stated and his is left to be understood. contigit is literally “touched” — of a traveller it means to reach, to make landfall on.

sentences.t:
Iamque malis annisque graves, dum prima retractant
fata domus releguntque suos sermone labores,
sentences.l: And now heavy with evils and with years, while they handle over again the first fates of [their] house and go back over their own labours in talk,
sentences.i: And now, weighed down by troubles and by years, while the two of them turn over again the early fortunes of their house and retrace their hardships in conversation,
sentences.n: graves is plural and the verbs are plural: the sentence has two old people in it, and it is Cadmus who speaks first. Both verbs are re- compounds of handling — retractant “handle again”, relegunt “gather (or read) back over” — and sermone, “in talk”, is a bare ablative where English needs a preposition. dum in the sense “while” takes a plain present indicative whatever the tense of the main clause, so the present here is the rule rather than a choice; the historic present, which Ovid does use in this part (ait, tendit, cadit, sibilat), is the separate thing that keeps the scene in front of the reader.

sentences.t:
“num sacer ille mea traiectus cuspide serpens”
Cadmus ait “fuerat, tum, cum Sidone profectus
vipereos sparsi per humum, nova semina, dentes?
sentences.l: “Had that serpent, run through by my spear-point, been a sacred one,” Cadmus says, “then, when, having set out from Sidon, I scattered over the ground the viper-teeth, new seeds?
sentences.i: “That serpent I ran through with my spear — was it a sacred thing,” Cadmus says, “back then, when I set out from Sidon and sowed the viper's teeth across the ground, a new kind of seed?
sentences.n: num introduces a question that expects the answer “no”; Cadmus is framing it as a denial he can no longer quite make, which is why it is frightening. The word order interlaces: sacer ille … serpens brackets mea traiectus cuspide, so the adjective and its noun stand at opposite ends with the participle phrase inside. nova semina is in apposition to dentes — the teeth are the seed, and that is the whole point of the sowing.

sentences.t:
Quem si cura deum tam certa vindicat ira,
ipse precor serpens in longam porrigar alvum.”
sentences.l: And if the gods' concern avenges him with anger so unerring, I myself, I pray, may be stretched out, a serpent, into a long belly.”
sentences.i: And if the gods' care is avenging him with anger so unfailing, then I pray that I myself may be drawn out, a serpent, into a long belly.”
sentences.n: Quem opening the sentence is a connecting relative: Latin habitually begins a new sentence with a relative pronoun where English begins with “and him” or “and as for it”. Read it as et eum, picking up serpens from the line before. deum is the contracted genitive plural, deorum, which verse prefers; porrigar is a present subjunctive of wish, with precor dropped in parenthetically — he is not asking politely, he is proposing his own sentence.

sentences.t:
Dixit, et ut serpens in longam tenditur alvum
durataeque cuti squamas increscere sentit
nigraque caeruleis variari corpora guttis.
sentences.l: He spoke; and as, a serpent, he is stretched out into a long belly, he feels scales grow onto his hardened skin and his black body be mottled with dark-blue drops.
sentences.i: He spoke; and as he is drawn out, a serpent, into a long belly, he feels the scales growing onto his hardened skin and his black body flecked with dark blue.
sentences.n: The prayer is granted in its own words: serpens in longam porrigar alvum at 575 comes back at once as ut serpens in longam tenditur alvum, with the wish's subjunctive replaced by a flat indicative. Nothing announces the god's consent — the repetition is the consent. durataeque cuti is a dative with increscere, “grow onto the hardened skin”, and nigra corpora is a poetic plural for one body, a licence verse takes constantly.

sentences.t:
In pectusque cadit pronus. Commissaque in unum
paulatim tereti tenuantur acumine crura.
sentences.l: And he falls forward upon his chest. And his legs, joined into one, are thinned little by little into a smooth-rounded point.
sentences.i: And he pitches forward onto his chest. His legs, fused into one, taper little by little to a smooth point.
sentences.n: In pectusque puts the -que on the second word of the phrase rather than the first: verse postpones the enclitic for the sake of the metre, and the “and” belongs to the front of the sentence. teres describes something turned smooth and round, as on a lathe — the tail is not merely pointed but finished. paulatim, “little by little”, is the word doing the work: Ovid times the change rather than simply reporting it.

sentences.t:
Bracchia iam restant: quae restant bracchia tendit
et lacrimis per adhuc humana fluentibus ora
“accede, o coniunx, accede, miserrima,” dixit
sentences.l: Now the arms remain: the arms that remain he stretches out, and with tears flowing over a face still human he said, “Come near, o wife, come near, most wretched one,”
sentences.i: The arms are what is left him: the arms that are left he holds out, and with the tears running down a face that is still human he said, “Come to me, wife — come to me, most wretched one,”
sentences.n: Bracchia iam restant: quae restant bracchia — the relative clause repeats the words of the main clause verbatim and in reverse order, naming the arms twice because they are about to stop being arms. lacrimis … fluentibus is an ablative absolute, a self-contained phrase “with tears flowing” where English wants a clause (“as the tears ran”); it takes no grammatical part in the main sentence, and per adhuc humana … ora sits inside it. You will meet the construction on nearly every page. Note also the gear-change of tense: tendit is a historic present, and then dixit drops into the perfect for the words themselves — Ovid runs the narration alongside you and steps back to report the speech.

sentences.t:
“dumque aliquid superest de me, me tange manumque
accipe, dum manus est, dum non totum occupat anguis!”
sentences.l: “and while something of me is left over, touch me and take [my] hand, while it is a hand, while the snake does not occupy the whole [of me]!”
sentences.i: “and while any part of me is left, touch me, take my hand while it is still a hand, while the snake has not taken all of me!”
sentences.n: Three dum-clauses in a row, each with a plain present indicative: dum in this sense means “during the time that it is still true that…”. They are a clock, and they narrow as they go — from something of me, to a hand, to the last of him — while the shortest of the three, dum manus est, sits in the middle where the loss is most nearly complete. totum is neuter and needs a word supplied — the whole of me — carried over from the me of the line before.

sentences.t:
Ille quidem vult plura loqui, sed lingua repente
in partes est fissa duas:
sentences.l: He indeed wants to speak more, but his tongue is suddenly split into two parts:
sentences.i: He would say more, but all at once his tongue is split in two:
sentences.n: quidem concedes before the sed reverses: “he does want to … but”. in partes est fissa duas splits its own phrase around the verb, the adjective duas stranded at the far end of the clause from its noun partes — the arrangement does to the words what the change does to the tongue.

sentences.t:
nec verba volenti
sufficiunt, quotiensque aliquos parat edere questus,
sibilat: hanc illi vocem natura reliquit.
sentences.l: nor do words suffice for [him] wanting [them], and as often as he makes ready to utter some complaints, he hisses: this voice nature has left him.
sentences.i: and words are not enough for him however he wants them; each time he sets himself to utter some lament, he hisses — this voice, and no other, nature has left him.
sentences.n: volenti is a bare present participle standing as a noun in the dative, “for [him] wanting”, with the person left to be inferred; English has to supply the pronoun, and the brackets in the literal mark where. hanc … vocem is thrown to the front for emphasis: this voice and no other. reliquit is exact and cruel — nature did not take his voice away, it left him one.

sentences.t:
Nuda manu feriens exclamat pectora coniunx
“Cadme, mane, teque, infelix, his exue monstris!
sentences.l: Striking her bare breast with her hand, his wife cries out: “Cadmus, stay, and strip yourself, unhappy man, of these monstrous shapes!
sentences.i: Beating her bare breast with her hand, his wife cries out: “Cadmus, wait — unhappy man, put off these monstrous shapes!
sentences.n: Nuda opens the line and pectora comes five words later, with manu feriens exclamat standing between the adjective and its noun; English cannot copy that spacing and has to put them back together. Beating the bare breast is the formal gesture of mourning, so she is grieving him before he is gone. exuo takes what is put off in the ablative — literally “strip yourself out of these monsters” — and monstrum is the same idea as the ostenta of 565 that drove him from the city: not a beast but a portent, a thing shown against nature.

sentences.t:
Cadme, quid hoc? ubi pes, ubi sunt umerique manusque
et color et facies et, dum loquor, omnia?
sentences.l: Cadmus, what [is] this? where is [your] foot, where are [your] shoulders and hands and colour and face and, while I am speaking, everything?
sentences.i: Cadmus, what is this? Where is your foot, where are your shoulders, your hands, your colour, your face — and, even as I speak, all of you?
sentences.n: quid hoc? has no verb: Latin drops est freely, and the omission makes the question a gasp rather than a sentence. Then the piling of -que … -que … et … et runs the parts together faster than she can name them and gives out into omnia, “everything”. dum loquor puts the loss inside the duration of her own sentence — more of him goes while she is asking where he has gone.

sentences.t:
cur non
me quoque, caelestes, in eandem vertitis anguem?”
sentences.l: why do you not turn me also, you heavenly ones, into the same snake?”
sentences.i: why do you not turn me too, you gods above, into the same serpent?”
sentences.n: quoque here is the adverb, “also” — but the identical letters are often quō-que, “and by which”, the ablative of the relative with -que attached, and the two have to be told apart by the sentence. caelestes is a vocative appeal to the gods above. eandem is feminine, so anguem is being treated as a feminine noun — anguis goes either way, and she asks to become the same snake in her own gender.

sentences.t:
Dixerat: ille suae lambebat coniugis ora
inque sinus caros, veluti cognosceret, ibat
et dabat amplexus adsuetaque colla petebat.
sentences.l: She had spoken: he was licking his wife's face, and going into her dear breast, as though he knew [her], and giving embraces and seeking the neck he was used to.
sentences.i: She had finished speaking. He was licking his wife's face, going to the breast he loved as though he knew her, giving embraces, seeking the neck he had always known.
sentences.n: Dixerat, the pluperfect, is Ovid's full stop after a speech — “she had spoken”, and the narrative moves. Four imperfects follow in a row (lambebat, ibat, dabat, petebat), the tense of action that goes on and on, so the caresses continue under the eyes of everyone watching. veluti cognosceret takes the subjunctive: “as if he recognised her”. The poem declines to say whether he does, and the whole weight of the scene rests on that refusal.

sentences.t:
Quisquis adest (aderant comites), terretur: at illa
lubrica permulcet cristati colla draconis.
sentences.l: Whoever is present — companions were present — is terrified: but she strokes the slippery neck of the crested serpent.
sentences.i: Everyone there is terrified — and there were companions there — but she strokes the slippery neck of the crested serpent.
sentences.n: The parenthesis exists to certify witnesses: the present adest for the general rule, the imperfect aderant to state as fact that people were standing there and saw it. lubrica … colla is again split around the verb, and colla is a poetic plural for one neck, like corpora at 578. cristati gives the creature the crest that Latin verse gives its serpents, so that the thing under her hand is a dragon of poetry and not a snake of the field.

sentences.t:
Et subito duo sunt iunctoque volumine serpunt,
donec in adpositi nemoris subiere latebras.
sentences.l: And suddenly they are two, and they glide with coil joined [to coil], until they went down into the hiding places of the grove close by.
sentences.i: And suddenly they are two, and they glide away with their coils entwined, until they slipped into the hiding places of the grove close at hand.
sentences.n: subiere is subierunt: the third-plural perfect in -ēre, which verse prefers for its shape and which you will meet on every page (meminere follows two lines later). Her own change is never narrated — duo sunt, “they are two”, is all the report there is, and it arrives between one clause and the next. iuncto volumine is a second ablative absolute, “with coil joined [to coil]”, standing where English wants a clause; and the tense turns from present to perfect at subiere, which is how the scene is closed.

sentences.t:
Nunc quoque nec fugiunt hominem nec vulnere laedunt
quidque prius fuerint, placidi meminere dracones.
sentences.l: Now too they neither flee from a human being nor injure [him] with a wound, and, peaceable serpents, they remember what they were before.
sentences.i: Even now they neither flee from a human being nor deal a wound; peaceable serpents, they remember what they once were.
sentences.n: meminere is meminerunt, the same -ēre perfect as subiere above; memini is one of the verbs whose perfect carries a present sense, so it is “they remember”, not “they remembered”. quid prius fuerint is an indirect question and therefore subjunctive. Nunc quoque is the adverb again, and it turns the whole tale into an explanation: the poem ends in the reader's own present tense, with the serpents of that country still gentle and the reason for it just told.

questions: House rendering candidate, IV.603 (the tale's closing sententia, often quoted on its own). Shipped l: “and, peaceable serpents, they remember what they were before.” Shipped i: “peaceable serpents, they remember what they once were.” Built from the Latin; recorded for ratification rather than re-decision.

Second house rendering candidate, IV.592–593a (Harmonia's “Cadme, quid hoc?”, anthologised on its own). Shipped l: “Cadmus, what [is] this? where is [your] foot, where are [your] shoulders and hands and colour and face and, while I am speaking, everything?” Shipped i: “Cadmus, what is this? Where is your foot, where are your shoulders, your hands, your colour, your face — and, even as I speak, all of you?”

Advisory: none shipped. The graphic-detail trigger was considered and declined. Ovid does dwell on the body limb by limb (576–589: scales, fused legs, forked tongue, lost voice), but this is transformation, not bodily damage — nothing is wounded, cut or destroyed — and the trigger names “bodily damage in specific detail” and says a close call is a no. The sexual-violence and present-day-group-aetiology triggers do not fire: the aetiology at 602–603 is of snakes in that country, not of any human group's body or character. Flagging the call in case the reviewer reads the transformation sequence differently.

Homograph: ora at 582 and 595 is the neuter plural of os, oris, “mouth, face” (poetic plural for one face), not ora, -ae, “shore, coast”, which is the sense the same form carries elsewhere in the poem.

Homograph: serpens at 575 and 576 is the noun “serpent” in apposition to the subject, and it is also, unchanged, the present participle of serpo, “crawling” — whose finite form serpunt appears at 600 in these same lines. Ovid is almost certainly hearing both.
Homograph: mane at 591 is the imperative of maneo, “stay, wait”, not the indeclinable noun mane, “morning”.
Homograph: sinus at 596 is accusative plural of sinus, “fold, breast, embrace”, not the “bay, gulf” sense the word carries in the poem's sea passages.
Variants: the supplied variants file is empty — the two witnesses agree throughout IV.563–603 — so no variant is mentioned anywhere in the apparatus.
No damaged digitization found in these lines; every form parses as Latin.

Convention question: at 594 eandem forces anguem to be feminine, while at 585 anguis has no agreement to show its gender. If the shared glossary fixes one gender for anguis, it should record that Ovid uses it both ways.

Reviewer, advisory: the drafter's no-advisory call is upheld. The part's sustained bodily description (576–589) is transformation, not damage — scales onto hardening skin, legs fusing to a point, a tongue splitting, a voice becoming a hiss. Nothing in these lines is wounded: the one piercing, traiectus cuspide at 571, is a single participle recalling an event outside the part, and the closing couplet says explicitly that these serpents deal no wound (nec vulnere laedunt, 602). The graphic-detail trigger asks for dwelling on bodily damage in specific detail and this is not that; the sexual-violence trigger does not fire; the aetiology at 602–603 is of a species of snake, not of any human group's body or character. Recorded so the call is visibly made rather than skipped.

Reviewer, house rendering: the two candidates the drafter recorded (IV.603 and IV.592–593a) were checked against the Latin and shipped unchanged. A third line in this part reads as quotable and should be ratified with them — IV.589, hanc illi vocem natura reliquit. Shipped l: “this voice nature has left him.” Shipped i: “this voice, and no other, nature has left him.” The “and no other” in the idiomatic renders the emphasis of the fronted hanc, which the note already identifies; if that is judged an addition rather than a rendering, the plain “this voice nature has left him” is the fallback.

Reviewer, IV.574: quem is the object of vindicat, not an objective genitive with cura. Both layers now read “the gods' care is avenging him”. Worth a ruling on whether cura deum here is the gods' concern for the dead serpent or their concern in the sense of watchful attention — the Latin supports either and Lectorium's rendering deliberately leaves it open.

Reviewer, IV.571: fuerat is pluperfect and the literal now shows it (“Had that serpent … been a sacred one”). Verse does sometimes use the pluperfect for a simple past, so a reader may meet editions and commentaries that treat it as “was”; Lectorium prints the tense that is there and lets the note carry the rest.
